extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, appellate practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative standards and doctrinal tests governing judicial remedial responses to procedurally or legally defective agency action (e.g., vacatur, remand, remand without vacatur, and harmless-error review). Geared to readers deciding or critiquing when and how courts should remedy agency error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chenery doctrine (requirement to base review on the agency’s grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative order cannot be upheld unless the grounds upon which the agency acted are those upon which its action can be sustained; courts may not uphold an agency action on new grounds not presented by the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chenery aims to assure that initial administrative determinations are made with relevant criteria in mind and in a proper procedural manner. The rule often commands remand when the agency’s stated reasons are inadequate. Cases and commentary debate its absoluteness and its interaction with harmless-error review; judges (e.g., Friendly) have emphasized limits to Chenery (e.g., avoiding a 'ping-pong game' of remands). Citations: SEC v. Chenery Corp., 318 U.S. 80 (1943); Friendly commentary; Wyman-Gordon, 394 U.S. 759.

rubrics_metrics.name: Massachusetts Trustees harmless-error exception to Chenery
rubrics_metrics.description: When an administrative mistake 'clearly had no bearing on the procedure used or the substance of decision reached,' the court may treat the mistake as harmless and need not remand for further agency explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Mass. Trs. of Eastern Gas & Fuel Assocs. v. United States, 377 U.S. 235 (1964). Courts sometimes invoke this to avoid pointless remands; Friendly called it a sound 'indentation' of Chenery. Use where the mistake is immaterial to the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless-error threshold — 'significant chance remand might lead to a different result'
rubrics_metrics.description: A remand is necessary only when the reviewing court concludes that there is a significant chance that but for the error the agency might have reached a different decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard, articulated by Judge Friendly and echoed in cases, requires courts to ask whether remand could realistically change the outcome; if not, error may be excused as harmless. Useful in contexts with well-developed records where outcome seems inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common circumstances warranting harmless-error treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors are most often held harmless when (1) the agency made a factual mistake of peripheral significance, or (2) the agency’s error is serious but the record so strongly supports the result that the court is confident the agency would reach the same decision on remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the two most prominent factual patterns (particularly in immigration and Social Security disability cases). Examples: PDK Labs (de minimis factual inaccuracies); Batson (discredited claimant testimony where other evidence undermined credibility). Courts should weigh the gravity of the error against the strength of the record support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Circuit / 'overwhelming evidence' standard for harmlessness
rubrics_metrics.description: An error cannot be harmless unless overwhelming evidence supporting the administrative adjudicator’s findings makes it clear that the same decision would have been reached in the absence of the errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulation from Cao He Lin v. U.S. Dep’t of Justice, 428 F.3d 391, 401 (2d Cir. 2005). Acts as a guardrail requiring a high confidence threshold before excusing error. Applied to prevent trivialization of Chenery’s remand rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: D.C. Circuit formulation — 'not the slightest uncertainty' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A court can affirm an agency decision for reasons not appearing in that decision only 'when there is not the slightest uncertainty as to the outcome of a proceeding on remand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by the D.C. Circuit (Grossmont Hosp. Corp. v. Burwell) to allow affirmance without remand but only when outcome on remand is virtually certain. Emphasizes strictness: only near-total confidence justifies skipping remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh Circuit / Spiva 'predictable with great confidence' formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is predictable with great confidence that the agency will reinstate its decision on remand because the decision is overwhelmingly supported by the record, then remanding is a waste of time and the court may affirm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Spiva v. Astrue, 628 F.3d 346, 353 (7th Cir. 2010). Similar to other high-confidence standards; rationale is avoiding futile remands that only delay resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ninth Circuit 'no reasonable ALJ could have reached a different' test
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is required when an ALJ fails to discuss competent testimony supporting the claimant’s position unless the court 'can confidently conclude that no reasonable ALJ, when fully crediting the testimony, could have reached a different disability determination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Stout v. Comm’r, Soc. Sec. Admin., 454 F.3d 1050, 1055–56 (9th Cir. 2006). This formulation ties harmlessness to a counterfactual standard: could any reasonable decisionmaker reach a different outcome?

rubrics_metrics.name: Allied-Signal balancing test for remand without vacatur
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision whether to vacate depends on 'the seriousness of the order's deficiencies (and thus the extent of doubt whether the agency chose correctly) and the disruptive consequences of an interim change that may itself be changed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Allied-Signal, Inc. v. U.S. NRC, 988 F.2d 146, 150–51 (D.C. Cir. 1993). Courts balance the gravity of the agency’s error against the practical harms (economic, regulatory, environmental) that vacatur would produce. Used to justify remand without vacatur when vacatur would be disproportionately disruptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory remedial framing — 'due account' for prejudicial error in the APA
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the APA directs courts to set aside unlawful agency action (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A)), it also requires that 'due account shall be taken of prejudicial error,' authorizing courts to consider harmlessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual argument that the APA contemplates harmless-error analysis for agency decisions, analogous to harmless-error doctrines in trial-court review. Used to rebut claims that courts lack statutory power to leave defective agency actions intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical and institutional factors courts should consider (guardrails)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should weigh agency diligence or negligence, the interest at stake, the type of error, the quality of the record, and agency resource constraints when deciding whether to vacate, remand, or hold an error harmless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article urges courts to try to measure tradeoffs (e.g., whether vacatur will improve agency behavior or simply slow adjudication). Suggested factors include whether front-line adjudicators can be incentivized, whether errors stem from scarce resources, and whether vacatur would meaningfully improve decision quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual patterns favoring remedial restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmless error and remand-without-vacatur are more common in relatively formal adjudicatory processes and in contexts with well-developed records (notably immigration and Social Security disability), where mistakes are frequent but the record often shows the claimant could not prevail on remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The observation that mass-adjudication settings and cases with strong existing records are typical circumstances where courts opt for remedial restraint. Use this context-sensitivity to guide remedial choices rather than applying a one-size-fits-all Chenery approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs-and-incentives consideration for remand without vacatur
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should assess whether vacating a rule would impose disproportionate costs, whether remanding without vacatur will leave the agency without incentive to respond, and whether forcing an agency to ‘fix’ minor mistakes wastes scarce agency resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical and doctrinal concerns: agencies may sit on remands for years, prompting mandamus; requiring full reprise of rulemaking can deplete agency resources and divert attention from urgent matters. The desirability of remand-without-vacatur depends on these practical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate uses of remand without vacatur
rubrics_metrics.description: Remand without vacatur may be appropriate when (a) preserving interim regulatory values outweighs correcting the error immediately, (b) the agency might reasonably reconsider the rule, or (c) plaintiffs seek more stringent regulation and prefer a flawed rule to none at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by North Carolina v. EPA and other cases where leaving a rule intact temporarily 'preserve[s] the environmental values covered' while the agency revises its rule. Courts should tailor remedial relief to the stakeholders’ interests and programmatic consequences.
